summary: Considers deficiencies of the 1988 X.500 standard that need to be addressed before an effective open Internet Directory can be built, focusing on replication. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: This memo lists replication requirements for a proposed Internet directory using X.500. It focuses on keeping directory knowledge and data available across multiple directory servers.

questions: what were the x.500 directory pilot scale targets
subtitle: Replication requirements for a distributed Internet directory based on X.500.

tldr.problem: The RFC identifies gaps in the 1988 X.500 standard that need solutions before a pilot Internet Directory can be deployed.
tldr.mechanism: It calls for replicating directory knowledge and data, referring users to alternate directory agents, and providing deployment guidance.
tldr.outcome: The memo sets scale targets for a pilot and does not specify an Internet standard.

today: RFC 1275 is Informational and examines requirements for an X.500 Internet Directory. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Distributed Directory Operation
sections.content:
The RFC considers deficiencies in the 1988 X.500 standard that it says must be addressed before an effective open Internet Directory can be established. It focuses on additional protocols or procedures needed for distributed operation.

The directory would run Directory Service Agents (DSAs) over TCP/IP using RFC 1006 and over an ISO Network Service. Distributed procedures should not require full connectivity.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo focuses on what X.500 would need to support a directory spread across many servers. It says that the system should not depend on every server being directly connected.

sections.title: Replicating Directory Knowledge
sections.content:
Knowledge information helps DSAs resolve names and perform searches. Knowledge high in the directory tree needs to be widely available. For example, a DSA resolving a name below Country=US needs complete knowledge at that point in the tree.

If only one or a few DSAs held this information, they could become bottlenecks. The RFC therefore calls for a systematic way to replicate knowledge across many DSAs.
sections.plainLanguage: Many directory servers need the information that tells them where names are held. Otherwise, a small number of servers could become bottlenecks.

sections.title: Replicating Data for Search
sections.content:
Searches at the root and country levels, including approximate matches for organization names, are important. Under the usual X.500 approach described here, subordinate references point to entries held by other DSAs, so one search may need to contact many servers.

The RFC says data replication is needed to make these searches reasonably efficient. It emphasizes replication high in the Directory Information Tree between different implementations; DSAs at lower levels may use implementation-specific techniques.
sections.plainLanguage: Some searches need to check information held by many servers. Keeping copies of important data high in the directory tree can make those searches more efficient.

sections.title: Alternate Servers and Scale
sections.content:
A DSA referral identifies only the master DSA, which the RFC says creates a single point of failure. The memo calls for allowing referrals to slave copies as well, to improve availability, and for guidelines that help a pilot use replication effectively.

The order of magnitude envisioned for the pilot is 100,000 non-leaf entries and several million leaf entries. The RFC says replication techniques have scaling limits and should not be pushed beyond them.
sections.plainLanguage: A referral should be able to point to copies as well as the master server. The memo also sets the approximate directory size expected for a pilot.

references.text: Rose, M. and D. Cass, "ISO Transport Services on top of the TCP", RFC 1006, May 1987.
